transcript: Header: 2025-06-11 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Marco Santos (Redwood) - Lena Ortiz, Samir Patel, Tina Huang, Raj (MapleAI)

Summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results vs their baseline provider. Focus on latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (rps), batching and quantization tradeoffs, next steps for deeper profiling and pricing. Medium transcription quality; some terms mis-transcribed.

00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run about 45 minutes. quick agenda: go over the benchmark spreadsheet, highlight where we saw wins/losses vs BaselineProvider, then tuning notes and next steps
00:23 Tina Huang: sounds good. i mainly want to see p99 numbers and any edge cases where tail latency spikes. our users are latency-sensitive for chat use case

00:35 Priya Nair: totally — we'll call out p50/p95/p99 and also token throughput at steady state. note that the test config we used was 8k context, 32k token limit, model rw-infer-13b-quant (approx), and concurrency stepped from 1 to 64 clients
00:50 Samir Patel: quick clarification: you said 8k context for everything? we usually do a mixed workload, some short replies ~50 tokens and some long generations ~800 tokens
01:05 Marco Santos: yep the sheet has mixed profile named 'maple-mix-1' — 70% short (<=100t) 30% long (~800t). the numbers i call out are aggregated but we have per-profile tabs
01:22 Lena Ortiz: i opened the spreadsheet, i see the 'redwood-vs-baseline-summary' tab. can you narrate the main takeaways?

01:30 Priya Nair: main takeaway: Redwood reduced p95 latency by ~33% vs BaselineProvider on the mixed workload. specific: Redwood p50 ~90ms, p95 ~280ms, p99 ~450ms. BaselineProvider p50 ~140ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~900ms (note some outliers on baseline due to GC and cold-starts)
02:05 Tina Huang: hmm p99 900ms is pretty high for them. were those cold-starts or sustained tail?

02:12 Marco Santos: mostly sustained tail under high concurrency. BaselineProvider showed queuing at the model runner when KV cache misses occurred — their prefix cache implementation wasn't as effective under our mix. we also saw tokenization differences: baseline tokenized the prompt less efficiently leading to more tokens generated
02:35 Samir Patel: do you have requests per second numbers? our target is 150 rps at 95% of traffic

02:40 Priya Nair: yes for the mixed workload Redwood sustained ~180 rps with median latencies in the 80-120ms range during steady state. BaselineProvider sustained ~120 rps before p95 ballooned above 400ms. throughput numbers are in the 'throughput' tab
03:05 Lena Ortiz: can you remind me what hardware you ran Redwood on?

03:10 Marco Santos: hosted run used g5a-equivalent GPUs (A10g-style) with our compilation/kernels tuned. Dedicated run we did on an NVIDIA H100 cluster for some heavier runs. BaselineProvider used a mix of older instances — they were on infer-late instances with different driver versions which explained some of the perf delta

03:30 Jordan Lee: also important: we tested quantized execute path (4-bit) on Redwood which reduced token cost by ~32% while preserving answer quality on our eval prompts. latency improved slightly due to smaller memory bandwidth pressure
03:48 Samir Patel: any quality regressions we should be worried about with quantization?
03:52 Priya Nair: minimal on our eval set. we ran 1k eval prompts comparing rouge/bleu-ish metrics and human spot checks; differences were marginal. we can share the eval deck
04:05 Tina Huang: where did caching help the most? prefix caching or KV cache?

04:12 Marco Santos: KV cache (prefix attention state) gave the biggest wins for repeated conversational turns. for our chat-heavy patterns, hit rate increased to ~65% after warmup which cut p50 by another 20-30ms on those requests
04:35 Samir Patel: BaselineProvider claimed they also have prefix caching — why didn't that show up?

04:40 Priya Nair: they do but in our runs their cache invalidation policy and placement led to more remote lookups; i.e., their cache wasn't colocated with the runner, adding network hops. we saw extra 80-200ms in some flows
05:05 Lena Ortiz: i noticed a row in the sheet labeled 'batching: 32 vs adaptive'. what's the recommendation there?

05:12 Marco Santos: adaptive batching on Redwood gave the best cost/latency tradeoff. fixed batch size of 32 increased throughput but hurt p95 for short prompts. adaptive batching keeps latency SLOs while improving token throughput

05:30 Jordan Lee: cost note: in our model profile, Redwood estimated $2.40 per 1M tokens for this workload (with quantization and caching gains). BaselineProvider was ~ $3.15 per 1M tokens in their public estimate for similar config. your accounting team may want the raw cost spreadsheet
05:55 Tina Huang: that's helpful, please send the cost breakdown. our budget team cares about steady-state $/qps not peak
06:05 Jordan Lee: will do — it's in the sheet but we'll also extract a one-pager
06:12 Samir Patel: curious about cold-start behavior. we saw baseline have multiple spikes after idle periods — what's Redwood's warmup strategy?

06:20 Priya Nair: our runtime keeps hot runners warm based on policy; for hosted we keep a small pool per model pinned to reduce cold starts. for private/dedicated you can configure minimum replication. that eliminated most of cold-start spikes in our tests
06:35 Lena Ortiz: are there any security or compliance gaps we should call out now? we have SOC2 and some internal requirements

06:42 Jordan Lee: we checked SOC2 attestation in the security tab. for Private deployment Redwood can run in your VPC with KMS integration and audit logs, which maps to your requirements — we can share the security binder
06:58 Tina Huang: please send that. also, separate question: how granular are rollouts? can we do canary and automatic fallback to smaller model if latency rises?

07:08 Marco Santos: yes, rollout policies support canary percentage, A/B, and automatic fallback to pinned model variants (e.g., 7b fallback) when SLOs breach. we tested automatic fallback in the POC and it avoided downtime during a synthetic load spike
07:30 Samir Patel: ok good. on the baseline sheet i see a few weird outliers around 900ms p99 — can you share raw traces?

07:40 Priya Nair: yes raw traces are in the sheet and the 'traces' folder in the shared drive; Jordan will attach a link. note: some of the baseline outliers correspond to container GC and their kernel mismatch
08:02 Tina Huang: any changes we'd need on our side to reproduce your config? docker images, model repo versions, sample scripts?

08:10 Marco Santos: we included a runbook: model id, runner image tag, open-source tokenizer versions. the main items are a) set batching policy to adaptive, b) enable 4-bit quant profile we used, c) configure cache co-location. Priya will share a short runbook

08:35 Jordan Lee: quick heads-up — we found one anomaly on day 2 where latency increased by ~10% due to a suboptimal kernel selection for that model size. we fixed the kernel selection rule and re-ran; improvements are reflected in the latest sheet
09:00 Lena Ortiz: for the 10k sample you want us to run, do you want full logs at debug level or trimmed metrics?
09:08 Priya Nair: full request/response traces for a subset (1000 requests) and aggregated metrics for the full 10k is ideal. that lets us map traces to spikes
09:22 Samir Patel: you mentioned quantization saved ~32% cost. is that consistent across long-response prompts?

09:30 Marco Santos: longer responses benefit similarly; memory footprint drops which allows higher batching. but on a tiny subset of prompts with very particular tokens there was a mild degeneration — we flagged them in the eval tab
09:55 Tina Huang: any thoughts on switching to Dedicated vs Hosted for our scale?

10:02 Jordan Lee: if you need predictable throughput and want to reserve capacity, Dedicated is the way. Hosted gives faster onboarding and marginally lower ops burden. cost-wise Dedicated has committed pricing that can be attractive once you cross sustained qps thresholds — we'll provide a model
10:30 Lena Ortiz: ok let's recap next steps

10:35 Jordan Lee: recap: 1) we'll share benchmark spreadsheet + raw traces (Jordan) 2) Priya to send runbook and quantization notes 3) MapleAI to run 10k sample and provide traces 4) schedule deep dive on VPC/routing. we'll aim to have the commercial proposal by Friday
10:55 Tina Huang: that works. thanks everyone
11:00 Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links and calendar invites
11:05 END TRANSCRIPT
